intro: You can already take part in meetings, describe trends in a chart and pause in clear chunks. Now you'll put it all together in a **presentation**: tell the audience where your talk is going (**signposting**), explain a chart so people really get the message, and handle **questions** calmly, even the ones you can't answer. Warm-up: when did you last give a presentation, and which part made you most nervous?
teachingNotes: This functional lesson (strand FN) builds on its chain; recap each in a line, don't re-teach: b2-meetings (Sorry to interrupt, but …; Sorry, could you clarify what you mean by …?; So what you're saying is …?; Bear with me for a second; I'll come to that in a minute; So, to sum up, …; the status / done / now / next update), b2-describing-data (trend verbs rise, fall, peak at, level off, remain stable, fluctuate; to = new level, by = size of change; sharply, steadily, slightly; twice as high as; 'until' only for time, never for a level; no 'was' before increased) and b2-pron-intonation-attitude (chunks with short silent pauses, slow down for numbers, stress the key word, a gentle rise for polite questions). New here: signposting a talk (opening, moving on, concluding), referring to visuals and giving their message, and handling audience questions honestly. Contexts: a startup in Jakarta, a bank in Surabaya, a thesis seminar on campus, a client pitch, Zoom presentations; Rina, Budi, Sari, Dimas, Pak Hasan, Bu Ani. All figures are practice figures.

Signposting (signpost = papan penunjuk jalan: phrases that tell listeners where they are in the talk). Opening: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming. / Today I'd like to talk about … (a phrase to remember: I'd like = I would like) / I've divided my talk into three parts. First, … Then, … Finally, … / Please feel free to ask questions at the end. Moving on: Let's move on to … / That brings me to … (also: That leads me to …) / Now let's look at … / Moving on to … . Concluding: To sum up, … / The key takeaway is that … (takeaway = the main message to remember; in British English a takeaway is also food you take home) / Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions. The node's common error: 'Okay, next. This is the graph.' → 'Let's move on to the results. As you can see in this graph, …': 'Okay, next' gives no direction and 'This is the graph' says what everybody can already see. Firstly / Secondly / Finally and First / Then / Finally are both fine; don't mark either wrong.

Indonesian presentation habits, named respectfully: (1) a long apology at the start, 'Mohon maaf kalau ada kesalahan' / 'Mohon maaf bahasa Inggris saya kurang bagus' → 'Sorry for my bad English' or 'Sorry if there are many mistakes'. In Indonesian culture it shows humility (rendah hati) and is polite; in English it makes the audience expect a weak talk before you begin. Show respect instead by thanking people and being well prepared. A short 'Sorry for the delay' for a real problem (the projector) is fine. (2) a long list of formal greetings (Yang terhormat Bapak …, Yang saya hormati …): in English, 'Good morning, everyone' is enough; at a very formal event you can name the most senior person first (Good morning, Professor Hasan, ladies and gentlemen). (3) reading slides word for word: the audience reads faster than you speak, so they stop listening. Keep few words on the slide and say the message in your own words. (4) closing with 'Mohon maaf apabila ada kata-kata yang kurang berkenan' → just 'Thank you for listening.'

Visuals: three moves. (a) Say what it shows: This chart / graph / table shows … (b) Point to the part: As you can see, … / If you look at the left-hand (right-hand) column, … / On the right, you can see … / Let's take a closer look at … (c) Give the message, with the trend language from b2-describing-data: What's interesting here is that … (a phrase to remember) / So, … / The figures speak for themselves (= the numbers are so clear that they need no explanation; use it only when that's true, and still say the number). 'As we can see' is also fine (Indonesian 'seperti yang bisa kita lihat'). left-hand column is common in British English; 'the left column' is also fine. column = kolom (top to bottom), row = baris (left to right). Speak in chunks and slow down for numbers (recap from the intonation lesson). Correct one thing: 'rose until 4,000' → rose to 4,000; 'This is the graph.' → say what it shows.

Audience questions: welcome (That's a great question. / Thanks for asking.), check if needed (If I understand correctly, you're asking … / Sorry, could you repeat the question? / recap: clarify what you mean by …), answer briefly, or be honest: I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll check and follow up by email. / I'll get back to you on that. (I'm afraid = sayangnya, a polite way to give bad news; NOT takut: Indonesian learners often read it as 'saya takut'.) Then check: Does that answer your question? (a gentle rise). Postpone politely: I'll come to that in a minute (recap) / Could we talk about that after the session? Don't bluff: guessing a number ('It's about two billion, I think, maybe') damages trust more than an honest 'I'll check'; in many Indonesian workplaces not knowing feels like losing face (malu, gengsi), but in English presentations an honest follow-up sounds professional. Avoid 'Do you understand?' / 'Is it clear or not?' after an answer: it can sound like a teacher checking a student.

Limits: A0–B1 grammar plus the chain (no third conditional, wish, past modals, participle clauses, non-defining relatives, causative, future perfect or advanced passive). Don't teach slide design, persuasion or sales-pitch techniques, storytelling, or body language in depth. Many choices are tendencies (To sum up / In conclusion / To conclude are all fine at the end of a talk): only mark clear errors wrong. Listening items use one voice and no speaker labels. Correct one thing at a time, usually 'Okay, next. This is the graph', an opening apology, reading the slide aloud, 'rose until', 'I'm afraid' read as takut, or a bluffed answer.

keyPoints.title: Signpost the structure of your talk
keyPoints.explanation: Signposts tell the audience where you are in your talk. Open with a greeting, the topic and a map: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about … / I've divided my talk into three parts. First, … Then, … Finally, …. Move from one part to the next with Let's move on to … / That brings me to …, not 'Okay, next'. Finish with To sum up, … / The key takeaway is that … / Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions. Skip the long opening apology ('Sorry for my bad English'): thank the audience instead.

examples.en: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.
examples.id: Selamat pagi semuanya, dan terima kasih sudah datang.

examples.en: That brings me to the second part: the costs.
examples.id: Itu membawa saya ke bagian kedua: biayanya.

examples.en: The key takeaway is that our customers want faster delivery.
examples.id: Pesan utamanya adalah pelanggan kita ingin pengiriman yang lebih cepat.

id.title: Menandai struktur presentasimu
id.explanation: Signpost (kalimat penunjuk arah) memberi tahu audiens kamu sedang di bagian mana. Buka dengan salam, topik dan peta presentasimu: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about … / I've divided my talk into three parts. First, … Then, … Finally, …. Pindah dari satu bagian ke bagian berikutnya dengan Let's move on to … / That brings me to …, bukan 'Okay, next'. Tutup dengan To sum up, … / The key takeaway is that … / Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions. Lewati permintaan maaf panjang di awal ('Sorry for my bad English'): ucapkan terima kasih kepada audiens saja.

keyPoints.title: Explain data and trends with visuals
keyPoints.explanation: Don't just say 'This is the graph' and don't read the slide word for word. Use three moves: say what the visual shows (This chart shows …), point to the part you mean (As you can see, … / If you look at the left-hand column, …) and give the message with trend words (rose sharply, peaked at, doubled, remained stable): What's interesting here is that …. Speak in chunks and slow down for the numbers.

examples.en: This chart shows our monthly sales in Surabaya last year.
examples.id: Grafik ini menunjukkan penjualan bulanan kita di Surabaya tahun lalu.

examples.en: As you can see, sales rose steadily and peaked in December.
examples.id: Seperti yang bisa Anda lihat, penjualan naik terus dan mencapai puncaknya di bulan Desember.

examples.en: What's interesting here is that weekend orders were twice as high as weekday orders.
examples.id: Yang menarik di sini adalah pesanan akhir pekan dua kali lebih tinggi daripada pesanan hari kerja.

id.title: Menjelaskan data dan tren dengan bantuan visual
id.explanation: Jangan cuma bilang 'This is the graph' dan jangan membaca slide kata per kata. Pakai tiga langkah: sebutkan apa yang ditunjukkan visualnya (This chart shows …), tunjuk bagian yang kamu maksud (As you can see, … / If you look at the left-hand column, …) dan sampaikan pesannya dengan kata-kata tren (rose sharply, peaked at, doubled, remained stable): What's interesting here is that …. Bicara per kelompok kata (chunk) dan pelan-pelan saat menyebut angka.

keyPoints.title: Handle audience questions
keyPoints.explanation: Welcome the question (That's a great question.), check it if you're not sure (If I understand correctly, you're asking …), answer briefly, then check back: Does that answer your question?. If you don't know, don't guess: I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll follow up by email. I'm afraid here means sayangnya (a polite way to give bad news), not takut.

examples.en: That's a great question. Thanks for asking.
examples.id: Pertanyaan yang bagus. Terima kasih sudah bertanya.

examples.en: If I understand correctly, you're asking about the price for next year?
examples.id: Kalau saya tidak salah tangkap, Anda bertanya soal harga untuk tahun depan?

examples.en: I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll follow up by email.
examples.id: Sayangnya saya tidak membawa angka itu, tapi akan saya kirimkan lewat email.

id.title: Menjawab pertanyaan audiens
id.explanation: Sambut pertanyaannya (That's a great question.), cek dulu kalau kamu tidak yakin (If I understand correctly, you're asking …), jawab dengan singkat, lalu cek kembali: Does that answer your question?. Kalau kamu tidak tahu, jangan menebak: I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll follow up by email. I'm afraid di sini artinya sayangnya (cara sopan menyampaikan kabar kurang enak), bukan takut.

guidedPractice.prompt: You're starting your talk at a campus seminar in Bandung. Complete with one word: Today I'd like to ___ about how students use food delivery apps.
You've finished the first part of your talk. Complete with one word: Let's move ___ to the survey results.
guidedPractice.hint: pindah ke bagian berikutnya = move … to

guidedPractice.prompt: Your next slide is a bar chart of monthly sales. Complete with one word: This chart ___ our monthly sales in 2024.
You want the audience to notice one surprising fact on the slide. Complete with one word: What's ___ here is that sales fell in June, not in January.
Someone asks a long question, and you want to check what they mean. Complete with one word: If I understand ___, you're asking about the delivery cost?

independentPractice.prompt: You don't know the answer to a question yet, but you'll find out. Complete with one word: Let me check, and I'll get ___ to you tomorrow.
independentPractice.hint: menghubungi lagi (dengan jawabannya) = get … to someone

independentPractice.prompt: Your chart shows that the new app went from 5,000 to 50,000 users in three months. The numbers are very clear. Complete with one word: The figures ___ for themselves.
You've reached the end of your talk. Thank the audience. Complete with one word: Thank you for ___.

assessment.prompt: You're presenting to a client in Surabaya. You've just told the audience that your talk has three parts. Now say which part comes first. Complete with one word: ___, I'll look at last year's sales. Then I'll talk about costs, and finally I'll show you our plan.
assessment.rubric: Correct: First (First, … Then, … Finally, …). 'Firstly' and 'First of all' = 100. 'To begin with' / 'To start with' = 100 (more than one word, but natural). 'Begin' or 'Start' = 30 (a verb, not a signpost: 'To begin, …' would be fine). 'One' = 40. 'Next' or 'Then' = 20 (the first part needs First). 'Today' = 30 (it doesn't show the order of the parts).

assessment.prompt: In your presentation at a bank in Jakarta, you've finished the part about costs. The next part is the timeline. Move on smoothly. Complete with one word: That ___ me to the timeline.
assessment.rubric: Correct: brings (That brings me to …). 'leads' (That leads me to …) = 100. 'takes' = 90 (understood and used, less common). 'bring' = 60 (That needs -s: brings). 'moves' = 40. 'next' or 'okay' = 10 (the node's common error 'Okay, next' gives no direction).

assessment.prompt: At the end of your talk about online shopping, you want to give the audience the one main message to remember. Complete with one word: The key ___ is that customers want faster delivery.
assessment.rubric: Correct: takeaway (The key takeaway is that … = the main message to remember). 'point', 'message', 'finding', 'lesson', 'idea', 'thing', 'issue', 'insight' = 100. 'conclusion' = 80 (understood; 'The main conclusion is …' is more usual). 'summary' = 50. 'key' alone or 'sum' = 20.

assessment.prompt: Your slide has a table of practice figures with two columns: the left column shows 2023 and the right column shows 2024. You want the audience to look at the 2024 figures. Complete with one word: If you look at the ___-hand column, you'll see the figures for 2024.
assessment.rubric: Correct: right (the right-hand column = kolom sebelah kanan, where 2024 is). 'left' = 0 (that column shows 2023). 'second' = 40 (understood, but it doesn't fit '-hand'). 'rigth' / 'rite' = 70 (the right word, misspelled).

assessment.prompt: Your slide shows online orders at a shop in Yogyakarta (practice figures): 2023: 10,000 · 2024: 20,000. Give the message in one exact verb in the past simple. Complete with one word: As you can see, online orders ___ in 2024.
assessment.rubric: Correct: doubled (10,000 → 20,000 = twice as many, the exact message). 'rose', 'increased', 'grew', 'went up' = 50 (true, but not exact: the slide's message is that orders doubled). 'double' = 60 (past simple needs -d). 'was doubled' or 'were doubled' = 40 (no 'was' here: the figure changed by itself). 'fell' or 'decreased' = 0.

assessment.prompt: After your talk about a new app, someone asks how many users it will have in 2030. Nobody can know that yet. Answer honestly and politely, without guessing. Complete with one word: I'm ___ I can't give you an exact number, but our target for next year is 50,000 users.
assessment.rubric: Correct: afraid (I'm afraid … = sayangnya, a polite way to give bad news). 'sorry' = 100. 'sure' = 20 ('I'm sure I can't …' sounds odd and isn't the polite softener). 'scared' = 20 (scared means takut: I'm afraid here is not about fear). 'afraid of' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani asked about the delivery times, and you've just explained them. Now check, politely, that your explanation was enough for her. Complete with one word: Does that ___ your question?
assessment.rubric: Correct: answer (Does that answer your question?). 'answers' = 60 (after Does, use the base form). 'reply' or 'respond' = 40 (they need 'to': 'reply to your question' is possible but not the set phrase). 'clear' = 30 ('Is that clear?' is a different sentence). 'understand' = 10.

blocks.text:
A **signpost** is a papan penunjuk jalan. In a presentation, **signposts** are short phrases that tell listeners **where they are** in your talk: what's coming, when one part ends and the next begins, and when you're finishing. Listeners can't scroll back like readers can, so they need these signs.

**Open:** greet, give the topic, then a **map** of the talk.
- ***Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.***
- ***Today I'd like to talk about …*** (a phrase to remember: *I'd like* = I would like, ingin)
- ***I've divided my talk into three parts. First, … Then, … Finally, …***
- ***Please feel free to ask questions at the end.***

**Move on** (pindah ke bagian berikutnya):
- ***Let's move on to …*** / ***Now let's look at …***
- ***That brings me to …*** (itu membawa saya ke …)

**Finish:**
- ***To sum up, …*** (recap from the meetings lesson)
- ***The key takeaway is that …*** (*takeaway* = the main message people take home; in British English a *takeaway* is also food you take home: makanan bungkus!)
- ***Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions.***

id.text:
**Signpost** artinya papan penunjuk jalan. Dalam presentasi, **signpost** adalah ungkapan pendek yang memberi tahu pendengar **mereka sedang di mana** dalam presentasimu: apa yang akan datang, kapan satu bagian selesai dan bagian berikutnya dimulai, dan kapan kamu akan selesai. Pendengar tidak bisa menggulir ke atas seperti pembaca, jadi mereka butuh tanda-tanda ini.

**Membuka:** beri salam, sebutkan topiknya, lalu **peta** presentasimu.
- ***Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.*** (selamat pagi semuanya, dan terima kasih sudah datang)
- ***Today I'd like to talk about …*** (ungkapan untuk dihafal: *I'd like* = I would like, ingin)
- ***I've divided my talk into three parts. First, … Then, … Finally, …*** (saya membagi presentasi saya menjadi tiga bagian. Pertama … Lalu … Terakhir …)
- ***Please feel free to ask questions at the end.*** (silakan bertanya di akhir)

**Pindah ke bagian berikutnya:**
- ***Let's move on to …*** / ***Now let's look at …*** (mari lanjut ke … / sekarang mari kita lihat …)
- ***That brings me to …*** (itu membawa saya ke …)

**Menutup:**
- ***To sum up, …*** (jadi, singkatnya; ulasan dari pelajaran rapat)
- ***The key takeaway is that …*** (*takeaway* = pesan utama yang dibawa pulang; dalam British English, *takeaway* juga berarti makanan bungkus!)
- ***Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions.*** (terima kasih sudah mendengarkan. Dengan senang hati saya menjawab pertanyaan)

rows.en: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about our new delivery service in Bandung.
rows.id: Selamat pagi semuanya. Hari ini saya ingin membahas layanan pengiriman baru kita di Bandung.

rows.id: Saya membagi presentasi saya menjadi tiga bagian: masalahnya, solusi kita dan biayanya.
rows.note: the map: the audience knows what's coming

id.note: petanya: audiens tahu apa yang akan datang

rows.en: So that's the problem. Now let's look at our solution.
rows.id: Jadi itulah masalahnya. Sekarang mari kita lihat solusinya.
rows.note: close one part, then open the next

id.note: tutup satu bagian, lalu buka bagian berikutnya

rows.id: Itu membawa saya ke poin terakhir saya: biayanya.

rows.en: To sum up, the new service is faster and only a little more expensive.

rows.en: Thank you for listening. I'm happy to take any questions.
rows.id: Terima kasih sudah mendengarkan. Dengan senang hati saya menjawab pertanyaan.

blocks.text:
Indonesian presentation habits to leave at home (with respect):
- **The long apology.** *Mohon maaf kalau ada kesalahan* or *Mohon maaf bahasa Inggris saya kurang bagus* is humble and polite in Indonesian. In English, `Sorry for my bad English` ✗ or `Sorry if there are many mistakes` ✗ at the start makes the audience expect a weak talk before you've begun. Show respect by **thanking** them and being well prepared. (A short *Sorry for the delay* for a real problem, like a slow projector, is fine.)
- **The long list of greetings.** *Yang terhormat Bapak …, yang saya hormati …* → in English, ***Good morning, everyone*** is enough. At a very formal event, name the most senior person first: *Good morning, Professor Hasan, ladies and gentlemen.*
- **`Okay, next. This is the graph.` ✗** *Okay, next* gives no direction, and everyone can see it's a graph. Say where you're going and what it shows: ***Let's move on to the results. As you can see in this graph, …***
- **The closing apology.** *Mohon maaf apabila ada kata-kata yang kurang berkenan* → just ***Thank you for listening.***

id.text:
Kebiasaan presentasi ala Indonesia yang sebaiknya ditinggal (dengan hormat):
- **Permintaan maaf yang panjang.** *Mohon maaf kalau ada kesalahan* atau *Mohon maaf bahasa Inggris saya kurang bagus* itu rendah hati dan sopan dalam bahasa Indonesia. Dalam bahasa Inggris, `Sorry for my bad English` ✗ atau `Sorry if there are many mistakes` ✗ di awal membuat audiens menduga presentasinya akan lemah, padahal kamu belum mulai. Tunjukkan rasa hormat dengan **berterima kasih** dan bersiap dengan baik. (*Sorry for the delay* yang singkat untuk masalah nyata, misalnya proyektor yang lambat, tidak apa-apa.)
- **Daftar salam yang panjang.** *Yang terhormat Bapak …, yang saya hormati …* → dalam bahasa Inggris, ***Good morning, everyone*** sudah cukup. Di acara yang sangat resmi, sebut orang paling senior lebih dulu: *Good morning, Professor Hasan, ladies and gentlemen.*
- **`Okay, next. This is the graph.` ✗** *Okay, next* tidak memberi arah, dan semua orang bisa melihat itu grafik. Katakan ke mana kamu pergi dan apa yang ditunjukkan: ***Let's move on to the results. As you can see in this graph, …***
- **Permintaan maaf di penutup.** *Mohon maaf apabila ada kata-kata yang kurang berkenan* → cukup ***Thank you for listening.***

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani is opening a presentation for new clients in Surabaya. Which opening sounds confident and polite?
options: Good morning, everyone. Before I start, sorry for my bad English and sorry if there are many mistakes.
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming. Today I'd like to talk about our new delivery service.
blocks.explain: It greets, thanks the audience and gives the topic (*Today I'd like to talk about …*). The first one is the Indonesian *mohon maaf* habit: in English it makes people expect a weak talk. The third one is too short and gives no greeting.

id.prompt: Bu Ani membuka presentasi untuk klien baru di Surabaya. Pembukaan mana yang terdengar percaya diri dan sopan?
id.explain: Pembukaan ini memberi salam, berterima kasih kepada audiens dan menyebutkan topiknya (*Today I'd like to talk about …*). Yang pertama adalah kebiasaan *mohon maaf* ala Indonesia: dalam bahasa Inggris itu membuat orang menduga presentasinya akan lemah. Yang ketiga terlalu singkat dan tanpa salam.

material.title: Talking about a chart or table

blocks.text:
A slide with a chart needs **three moves** from you:
1. **Say what it shows:** ***This chart / graph / table shows …***
2. **Point to the part you mean:** ***As you can see, …*** / ***If you look at the left-hand column, …*** / ***On the right, you can see …*** / ***Let's take a closer look at …***
3. **Give the message** (the 'so what?'): ***What's interesting here is that …*** (a phrase to remember) / ***So, …***

For move 3, use the trend language from the graphs lesson: *rose sharply, fell slightly, peaked at, remained stable, doubled, twice as high as*. Remember: **to** + the new level, **by** + the size of the change, and **until** only for time.

A **column** is a kolom (top to bottom); a **row** is a baris (left to right). *left-hand column* is common in British English; *the left column* is fine too.

***The figures speak for themselves*** = the numbers are so clear that they need no explanation. Use it only when that's true, and still say the key number.

Recap from the intonation lesson: say numbers in **chunks**, slowly, with a short silent pause: *In 2024 | online orders | doubled.*

id.text:
Slide yang berisi grafik butuh **tiga langkah** darimu:
1. **Sebutkan apa yang ditunjukkan:** ***This chart / graph / table shows …*** (grafik / tabel ini menunjukkan …)
2. **Tunjuk bagian yang kamu maksud:** ***As you can see, …*** (seperti yang bisa Anda lihat) / ***If you look at the left-hand column, …*** (kalau Anda melihat kolom sebelah kiri) / ***On the right, you can see …*** (di sebelah kanan, Anda bisa melihat …) / ***Let's take a closer look at …*** (mari kita lihat lebih dekat …)
3. **Sampaikan pesannya** (lalu kenapa?): ***What's interesting here is that …*** (yang menarik di sini adalah …; ungkapan untuk dihafal) / ***So, …***

Untuk langkah 3, pakai bahasa tren dari pelajaran grafik: *rose sharply, fell slightly, peaked at, remained stable, doubled, twice as high as*. Ingat: **to** + level barunya, **by** + besarnya perubahan, dan **until** hanya untuk waktu.

**Column** adalah kolom (dari atas ke bawah); **row** adalah baris (dari kiri ke kanan). *left-hand column* umum di British English; *the left column* juga boleh.

***The figures speak for themselves*** = angkanya sudah sangat jelas sehingga tidak perlu dijelaskan. Pakai hanya kalau memang benar begitu, dan tetap sebutkan angka utamanya.

Ulasan dari pelajaran intonasi: ucapkan angka per **chunk** (kelompok kata), pelan-pelan, dengan jeda singkat tanpa suara: *In 2024 | online orders | doubled.*

rows.en: This graph shows the number of app users in Bandung from January to October.
rows.id: Grafik ini menunjukkan jumlah pengguna aplikasi di Bandung dari Januari sampai Oktober.

rows.en: As you can see, the number of users rose steadily until July.
rows.id: Seperti yang bisa Anda lihat, jumlah pengguna naik terus sampai bulan Juli.

rows.en: If you look at the left-hand column, you can see last year's prices.
rows.id: Kalau Anda melihat kolom sebelah kiri, Anda bisa melihat harga tahun lalu.

rows.en: What's interesting here is that sales in Medan were twice as high as in Makassar.
rows.id: Yang menarik di sini adalah penjualan di Medan dua kali lebih tinggi daripada di Makassar.

rows.en: In three months, the number of complaints fell by half. The figures speak for themselves.
rows.id: Dalam tiga bulan, jumlah keluhan turun setengahnya. Angkanya sudah berbicara sendiri.

blocks.text:
Indonesian trap: **reading the slide word for word.** Many of us fill slides with text and read it aloud, often facing the screen. The audience reads faster than you speak, so they stop listening to you. Keep only a few words on the slide, look at the audience, and **say the message in your own words**. Your slide says *Q3 revenue: Rp4.2 billion (+15%)*; you say: *As you can see, revenue rose by fifteen percent in the third quarter.*
And a recap: `rose until 4,000` ✗ (*naik sampai*) → **rose to 4,000**.

id.text:
Jebakan dari kebiasaan kita: **membaca slide kata per kata.** Banyak dari kita mengisi slide dengan teks lalu membacanya keras-keras, sering sambil menghadap layar. Audiens membaca lebih cepat daripada kamu bicara, jadi mereka berhenti mendengarkanmu. Taruh hanya sedikit kata di slide, lihat ke audiens, dan **sampaikan pesannya dengan kata-katamu sendiri**. Slide-mu bertuliskan *Q3 revenue: Rp4.2 billion (+15%)*; kamu bilang: *As you can see, revenue rose by fifteen percent in the third quarter.*
Dan ulasan: `rose until 4,000` ✗ (*naik sampai*) → **rose to 4,000**.

blocks.prompt: Your slide says: 'Q3 revenue: Rp4.2 billion (+15%)'. What's the best thing to say?
options: Q3 revenue, Rp4.2 billion, plus fifteen percent.
As you can see, revenue rose by fifteen percent in the third quarter, to 4.2 billion rupiah.
This is the revenue. You can read it.
blocks.explain: It points to the slide (*As you can see*) and gives the message as a full sentence, with **by** for the size of the change and **to** for the new level. The first one just reads the slide aloud; the third one says what everyone can already see.

id.prompt: Slide-mu bertuliskan: 'Q3 revenue: Rp4.2 billion (+15%)'. Apa yang paling baik untuk dikatakan?
id.explain: Kalimat ini menunjuk slide-nya (*As you can see*) dan menyampaikan pesannya dalam kalimat lengkap, dengan **by** untuk besarnya perubahan dan **to** untuk level barunya. Yang pertama hanya membaca slide; yang ketiga hanya mengatakan apa yang sudah bisa dilihat semua orang.

blocks.text:
Q&A (questions and answers, sesi tanya jawab) scares many presenters. A simple plan helps:
1. **Welcome the question:** ***That's a great question.*** / ***Thanks for asking.***
2. **Check it, if you're not sure:** ***If I understand correctly, you're asking …?*** / ***Sorry, could you repeat the question?*** (recap from the meetings lesson: *clarify what you mean by …*)
3. **Answer briefly**, or **be honest** if you don't know: ***I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll follow up by email.*** / ***I'll check and get back to you on that.***
4. **Check back:** ***Does that answer your question?*** (with a gentle rise ↗, as in the intonation lesson)

If the question is about a later part of your talk: ***I'll come to that in a minute.*** If it's off topic or very long: ***Could we talk about that after the session?***

**Don't bluff** (don't pretend to know). A guessed number that later turns out wrong hurts your credibility much more than an honest *I'll check*.

id.text:
Q&A (questions and answers, sesi tanya jawab) membuat banyak presenter takut. Rencana sederhana ini membantu:
1. **Sambut pertanyaannya:** ***That's a great question.*** (pertanyaan yang bagus) / ***Thanks for asking.*** (terima kasih sudah bertanya)
2. **Cek dulu, kalau kamu tidak yakin:** ***If I understand correctly, you're asking …?*** (kalau saya tidak salah tangkap, Anda bertanya …?) / ***Sorry, could you repeat the question?*** (ulasan dari pelajaran rapat: *clarify what you mean by …*)
3. **Jawab dengan singkat**, atau **jujur** kalau kamu tidak tahu: ***I'm afraid I don't have that figure with me, but I'll follow up by email.*** (sayangnya saya tidak membawa angka itu, tapi akan saya kirimkan lewat email) / ***I'll check and get back to you on that.*** (akan saya cek lalu saya kabari)
4. **Cek kembali:** ***Does that answer your question?*** (apakah itu menjawab pertanyaan Anda?; dengan nada naik yang lembut ↗, seperti di pelajaran intonasi)

Kalau pertanyaannya tentang bagian presentasi yang belum dibahas: ***I'll come to that in a minute.*** (nanti saya bahas) Kalau di luar topik atau sangat panjang: ***Could we talk about that after the session?*** (bisa kita bahas setelah sesi ini?)

**Jangan bluffing** (pura-pura tahu). Angka tebakan yang ternyata salah merusak kepercayaan orang jauh lebih parah daripada *I'll check* yang jujur.

rows.en: That's a great question, Pak Hasan. Thanks for asking.
rows.id: Pertanyaan yang bagus, Pak Hasan. Terima kasih sudah bertanya.

rows.en: If I understand correctly, you're asking whether the app works offline?
rows.id: Kalau saya tidak salah tangkap, Anda bertanya apakah aplikasinya bisa dipakai offline?
rows.note: whether = apakah, as in indirect questions

id.note: whether = apakah, seperti di indirect questions (pertanyaan tidak langsung)

rows.en: I'm afraid I don't know the exact number, but I'll check and get back to you.
rows.id: Sayangnya saya tidak tahu angka pastinya, tapi akan saya cek lalu saya kabari.

rows.en: Good point. I'll come to that in a minute, in the part about costs.
rows.id: Poin yang bagus. Nanti saya bahas sebentar lagi, di bagian tentang biaya.

rows.en: So the price stays the same until December. Does that answer your question?
rows.id: Jadi harganya tetap sama sampai Desember. Apakah itu menjawab pertanyaan Anda?

blocks.text:
Two traps:
- **I'm afraid ≠ saya takut.** In *I'm afraid I don't know*, *afraid* doesn't mean fear. It's a polite way to give bad news, like *sayangnya* or *mohon maaf, …*. You'll hear it everywhere: *I'm afraid the train is delayed.*
- **Not knowing isn't shameful.** In many offices, not knowing the answer in front of the boss feels like losing face (malu, gengsi), so presenters guess: `It's about two billion, I think, maybe` ✗. In English presentations, an honest ***I'll check and follow up by email*** sounds professional, as long as you really send that email.
Also avoid `Do you understand?` or `Is it clear or not?` after your answer: it can sound like a teacher checking a student. Ask ***Does that answer your question?***

id.text:
Dua jebakan:
- **I'm afraid ≠ saya takut.** Dalam *I'm afraid I don't know*, *afraid* tidak berarti takut. Itu cara sopan menyampaikan kabar kurang enak, seperti *sayangnya* atau *mohon maaf, …*. Kamu akan sering mendengarnya: *I'm afraid the train is delayed.* (mohon maaf, keretanya terlambat)
- **Tidak tahu itu tidak memalukan.** Di banyak kantor, tidak tahu jawabannya di depan atasan terasa seperti kehilangan muka (malu, gengsi), jadi presenter menebak: `It's about two billion, I think, maybe` ✗. Dalam presentasi berbahasa Inggris, ***I'll check and follow up by email*** yang jujur terdengar profesional, asalkan kamu benar-benar mengirim email itu.
Hindari juga `Do you understand?` atau `Is it clear or not?` setelah menjawab: bisa terdengar seperti guru yang mengecek murid. Tanyakan ***Does that answer your question?***

blocks.prompt: A presenter says: 'I'm afraid I don't have the exact number.' What does she mean?
options: She is scared of the number.
She is politely saying that she doesn't have the number.
She has the number, but she doesn't want to say it.
blocks.explain: *I'm afraid …* is a polite way to give bad news, like *sayangnya*. It has nothing to do with fear (takut), and she isn't hiding anything: she really doesn't have the number.

id.prompt: Seorang presenter bilang: 'I'm afraid I don't have the exact number.' Apa maksudnya?
id.explain: *I'm afraid …* adalah cara sopan menyampaikan kabar kurang enak, seperti *sayangnya*. Tidak ada hubungannya dengan takut, dan dia tidak menyembunyikan apa-apa: dia memang tidak punya angkanya.
options: Dia mengatakan dengan sopan bahwa ia tidak punya angkanya.
Dia punya angkanya, tetapi tidak ingin menyebutkannya.

blocks.text:
Here's the skeleton of a short presentation by Rina, a product manager at a startup in Jakarta, to her company's managers. Find the opening, the map, a transition, the chart, the conclusion and the Q&A. The chart, as a table (practice figures): orders per month through the new app, **January 8,000 · March 12,000 · May 16,000**.

To prepare your own talk: write the signposts first (they're the skeleton), mark the pauses with | (recap from the intonation lesson), and practise answering the three questions you're most afraid of.

id.text:
Ini kerangka presentasi singkat oleh Rina, seorang product manager di sebuah startup di Jakarta, untuk para manajer di perusahaannya. Temukan pembukaan, peta presentasi, perpindahan bagian, grafiknya, kesimpulan dan sesi tanya jawabnya. Grafiknya, dalam bentuk tabel (angka latihan): pesanan per bulan lewat aplikasi baru, **Januari 8.000 · Maret 12.000 · Mei 16.000**.

Untuk menyiapkan presentasimu sendiri: tulis signpost-nya dulu (itu kerangkanya), tandai jedanya dengan | (ulasan dari pelajaran intonasi), dan berlatih menjawab tiga pertanyaan yang paling kamu takutkan.

rows.en: Good afternoon, everyone, and thanks for coming. Today I'd like to talk about our new app.
rows.id: Selamat siang semuanya, dan terima kasih sudah datang. Hari ini saya ingin membahas aplikasi baru kita.

id.note: pembukaan: salam + topik, tanpa minta maaf

rows.en: I've divided my talk into two parts: the results so far and our plan for next year.
rows.id: Saya membagi presentasi saya menjadi dua bagian: hasil sejauh ini dan rencana kita untuk tahun depan.

rows.en: This chart shows our monthly orders. As you can see, orders doubled between January and May.
rows.id: Grafik ini menunjukkan pesanan bulanan kita. Seperti yang bisa Anda lihat, pesanan naik dua kali lipat antara Januari dan Mei.
rows.note: the visual: what it shows + the message

rows.en: That brings me to the second part: our plan for next year.
rows.id: Itu membawa saya ke bagian kedua: rencana kita untuk tahun depan.

rows.en: To sum up, the app is growing fast, and the key takeaway is that we need more drivers.
rows.id: Singkatnya, aplikasinya tumbuh cepat, dan pesan utamanya adalah kita butuh lebih banyak pengemudi.

rows.en: That's a great question, Bu Ani. I'm afraid I don't have the costs for each city with me, but I'll send them to you today.
rows.id: Pertanyaan yang bagus, Bu Ani. Sayangnya saya tidak membawa biaya untuk setiap kota, tapi akan saya kirimkan hari ini.

id.note: tanya jawab: sambutan + jawaban jujur + tindak lanjut

blocks.prompt: When would a presenter say 'That brings me to my last point'?
options: At the very start, before the topic.
When moving from one part of the talk to the next (here, the last part).
When answering a question from the audience.
blocks.explain: *That brings me to …* is a transition: it closes one part and opens the next. At the start you greet and give the topic and the map; in the Q&A you welcome, answer and check back.

id.prompt: Kapan seorang presenter mengatakan 'That brings me to my last point'?
id.explain: *That brings me to …* adalah ungkapan perpindahan: menutup satu bagian dan membuka bagian berikutnya. Di awal kamu memberi salam, menyebut topik dan peta presentasi; di sesi tanya jawab kamu menyambut, menjawab dan mengecek kembali.
options: Pada awal sekali, sebelum menyampaikan topik.
Saat berpindah ke bagian berikutnya (di sini, bagian terakhir).

suggestedQuestions: Is it rude not to apologise for my English at the start?
What can I say instead of 'Okay, next slide'?
How do I talk about a chart without reading the slide?
What should I say when I don't know the answer to a question?

resources.title: How to give a strong presentation: tips & key phrases
resources.note: Tips for structuring a presentation clearly, with key phrases such as begin by, move on to, refer to and conclude with. Good for nervous speakers.

id.note: Tips untuk menyusun presentasi dengan jelas, dengan ungkapan penting seperti begin by, move on to, refer to dan conclude with. Cocok untuk yang sering gugup.

resources.title: How to Give an Informative Presentation: What to say and do
resources.note: Phrases for each part of a presentation, plus how to handle difficult questions (buying time, asking for a repeat, saying you don't have the information). engVid marks it as advanced, so some phrases go beyond this lesson.

id.note: Ungkapan untuk setiap bagian presentasi, plus cara menghadapi pertanyaan sulit (mengulur waktu, meminta pertanyaan diulang, mengatakan bahwa kamu tidak punya informasinya). engVid menandainya sebagai tingkat lanjut, jadi beberapa ungkapannya di atas level pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Kamu sudah bisa ikut rapat, mendeskripsikan tren dalam grafik dan memberi jeda per kelompok kata dengan jelas. Sekarang kamu menggabungkan semuanya dalam sebuah **presentasi**: memberi tahu audiens ke mana arah presentasimu (**signposting**), menjelaskan grafik supaya pesannya benar-benar sampai, dan menjawab **pertanyaan** dengan tenang, termasuk yang tidak bisa kamu jawab. Pemanasan: kapan terakhir kali kamu presentasi, dan bagian mana yang paling membuatmu gugup?
suggestedQuestions: Apakah tidak sopan kalau aku tidak minta maaf soal bahasa Inggrisku di awal?
Apa yang bisa aku katakan selain 'Okay, next slide'?
Bagaimana cara membahas grafik tanpa membaca slide-nya?
Apa yang harus aku katakan kalau tidak tahu jawaban sebuah pertanyaan?

assessment.pres-1: Kamu presentasi untuk klien di Surabaya. Kamu baru saja bilang kepada audiens bahwa presentasimu punya tiga bagian. Sekarang sebutkan bagian mana yang pertama. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: ___, I'll look at last year's sales. Then I'll talk about costs, and finally I'll show you our plan.
assessment.pres-2: Dalam presentasimu di sebuah bank di Jakarta, kamu sudah selesai membahas biaya. Bagian berikutnya adalah jadwal (timeline). Pindah bagian dengan mulus. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: That ___ me to the timeline.
assessment.pres-3: Di akhir presentasimu tentang belanja online, kamu ingin memberi audiens satu pesan utama untuk diingat. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: The key ___ is that customers want faster delivery.
assessment.pres-4: Slide-mu berisi tabel angka latihan dengan dua kolom: kolom kiri untuk 2023 dan kolom kanan untuk 2024. Kamu ingin audiens melihat angka tahun 2024. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: If you look at the ___-hand column, you'll see the figures for 2024.
assessment.pres-5: Slide-mu menunjukkan pesanan online di sebuah toko di Yogyakarta (angka latihan): 2023: 10.000 · 2024: 20.000. Sampaikan pesannya dengan satu kata kerja yang tepat dalam past simple. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: As you can see, online orders ___ in 2024.
assessment.pres-6: Setelah presentasimu tentang aplikasi baru, seseorang bertanya berapa jumlah penggunanya di tahun 2030. Belum ada yang bisa tahu. Jawab dengan jujur dan sopan, tanpa menebak. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: I'm ___ I can't give you an exact number, but our target for next year is 50,000 users.
assessment.pres-7: Bu Ani bertanya soal waktu pengiriman, dan kamu baru saja menjelaskannya. Sekarang cek dengan sopan apakah penjelasanmu sudah cukup baginya. Lengkapi dengan satu kata: Does that ___ your question?
